info.name: csph-services-direct
info.description:
# CSPH - services-direct collection (each service on its own port)

Every request targets a service's **own port** rather than going through the gateway - the local equivalent of
`http://csph/gpl-<service>/...` inside Kubernetes.

## Why

`PermissionAspect` (common-lib) checks `GplSecurityContext.isAuthenticated()` first, and that flag is only true when
`GplSecurityContextFilter` has seen a non-empty **`X-User-PersonId`** header. With no header there is no security
context, the aspect logs "internal call, pass-through" and proceeds.

So a direct-port request with no `X-User-PersonId` exercises the full endpoint surface with **no permission
constraint** - useful for exploring the API, generating fixtures, and debugging a route without having to log in.
Folder `10 - Permission AOP contrast` proves the mechanism with three requests.

**The flip side is in that same folder: the headers are trusted.** Never expose these ports outside the cluster.

## Headers

| case | headers sent |
| --- | --- |
| reads | none - this is the bypass |
| writes declaring `@RequestHeader("X-User-PersonId")` (organization-service, roles, groups, auth logout) | `X-User-PersonId` only |
| `GET /api/v1/me`, `/me/permissions` | `X-User-PersonId` - the controller throws 401 without it |
| everything else | none |

`Authorization` is never sent. auth-service permits `/api/v1/auth/**` and `/api/v1/me/**` in its own
`SecurityConfig`; every other service has no security chain at all.

## Coverage

Read + create + one domain action per service, plus folder `00` reachability probes for all ten ports and folder
`10` for the AOP contrast. The full CRUD surface lives in `csph-gateway` - this collection is the diagnostic view,
not a second copy of it.

item.name: 00 - README

request.description:
Direct probe of **auth-service** on its own port (8081) - the in-cluster equivalent of
`http://csph/gpl-auth-service/api/v1/me`.

Sent with **no security headers at all**, which is the point of this collection: `PermissionAspect` finds no
`GplSecurityContext` and passes the call straight through, so a `200` here proves both that the port is open and
that the permission check was bypassed.

- `200` - reachable, and the endpoint is genuinely open (or the check was skipped)
- `401` - reachable, and the endpoint genuinely requires a caller (`/api/v1/me` without `X-User-PersonId`, for example)
- `404` - reachable, but that path is not mapped in this service

item.description:
One probe per port, so a single pass tells you which of the nine services (and the gateway) are actually up.

Every assertion is deliberately loose - `200`, `401` or `404` all pass. The goal is reachability, not correctness:
a `Connection refused` here means the container is down, and every later folder will fail for that reason rather
than a real one.

item.name: 01 - Auth  (direct -8081)

request.description:
**auth-service on :8081**, hit directly. In Kubernetes this is `http://csph/gpl-auth-service/api/v1/auth/login`.

No `Authorization` header is needed: `auth-service` is the one service with a Spring Security filter chain, and
`SecurityConfig` marks `/api/v1/auth/**` `permitAll()`. Every other service has no security chain at all.

`ipAddress` and `deviceInfo` are sent here for the same reason as in the gateway collection - the `refresh_tokens`
row written by this call is shared with the gateway call, and a short `ip_address` overflows its column on the next
login. Keep the values realistic.

The tokens returned are **not** stored: with no gateway there is nothing to consume them, and this collection's whole
premise is not needing one. The test still decodes the JWT so you can see the claims.

**auth-service on :8081**.

This is the one direct-port read that *does* need `X-User-PersonId`, and for a different reason than the permission
bypass: `MeController.requireCurrentUser` throws `UnauthorizedException` when the header is absent or blank. That
maps to 401 through `GlobalExceptionHandler`, not to a bypass - the controller is doing the check itself, before any
aspect could.

So this request is the exception that proves the rule: the header is not a permission token, it is a *required
request parameter* on this particular route.

`roles` is split out of the `X-User-Roles` header - which nothing populates on a direct call, so it is `[]` here. In
the gateway collection the same endpoint returns the JWT's roles. That difference is the whole point of the two
collections.

**auth-service on :8081**.

The same split-the-header behaviour as `/me`, on the `X-User-Permissions` header. On a direct call nothing populates
that header, so the result is `[]` - whereas through the gateway it holds every permission resolved at login.

This pair (`/me` and `/me/permissions` returning empty role/permission arrays) is the cleanest demonstration in the
suite that these two endpoints are **header readers, not database readers**. They compute nothing.

**auth-service on :8081**. Last request in this folder.

`AuthService.logout` deletes **every** refresh token for the person, and the database is shared with the gateway
collection. So running this invalidates the `refreshToken` that `csph-gateway > 01 - Auth` captured. Re-run that
folder''s login + refresh if you then use the gateway collection.

`X-User-PersonId` is a required `@RequestHeader` here - no `required = false` - so it is sent.

item.description:
auth-service on **8081**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-auth-service` in-cluster.

auth-service is the only service with a Spring Security filter chain, and it permits `/api/v1/auth/**` and
`/api/v1/me/**` outright - so no JWT is needed for anything in this folder.

Note that `/me` and `/me/permissions` return **empty** role and permission arrays here even for a superadmin: they
read the `X-User-Roles` / `X-User-Permissions` headers, and on a direct call nothing populates those headers. Same
requests through the gateway return the real thing.

item.name: 02 - Organization  (direct -8082)

request.description:
**organization-service on :8082**, sent with **no security headers**. `@RequiresPermission("ORG_VIEW")` is on this
method, and it is skipped: `PermissionAspect` sees no `GplSecurityContext` and proceeds.

**Bare `PageResponse`** - no `success` envelope, exactly as through the gateway. Response shape is a controller
decision and has nothing to do with the route taken.

Also the org bootstrap for this collection: captures `orgId`, `marketerOrgId`, `transporterOrgId`, `clientOrgId`
leniently on `type`, and `siteId` / `siteIdDest` from the sites list two requests below.

**organization-service on :8082**, no security headers, so `ORG_VIEW` is bypassed.

`{orgId}` is the UUID primary key captured above - not the business `code`.

**organization-service on :8082**, with `X-User-PersonId`.

`OrganizationController.createOrganization` declares `@RequestHeader("X-User-PersonId") String userId` with **no
`required = false`** - so on this endpoint the header is not a permission token, it is a mandatory request
parameter. Omit it and you get 400 `MissingRequestHeaderException`, never a 403.

This is the single most important thing to know when working against the direct ports: **the bypass in
`PermissionAspect` is not the same as "no headers needed"**. Required `@RequestHeader`s are enforced by Spring MVC
before the aspect ever runs.

`code` carries `{{uniq}}` because `Organization.code` is `UNIQUE` - the same reason the gateway collection does it,
and the reason both collections can be re-run against one database.

**organization-service on :8082**, with `X-User-PersonId` (required `@RequestHeader`).

`UpdateStatusRequest` = `{newStatus, reason}`, and `OrganizationService.updateStatus` is a plain setter with no enum
validation - the same `{newStatus, reason}` shape appears in user-service too, with a matching contract.

This is the "one domain action" for organization-service: the status lifecycle, which is the write every entity in
the platform shares.

**organization-service on :8082**, no security headers, so `ORG_VIEW` is bypassed.

Enveloped **array** (`ApiResponse<List<OrganizationSummaryResponse>>`) - a third response shape in this one
controller, alongside the bare page and the enveloped object. Empty for the org just created, which is correct: it
has no children.

**organization-service on :8082**, no security headers, so `SITE_VIEW` is bypassed.

**Bare `PageResponse`** again, like `/organizations` directly above. Captures `siteId` (row 0) and `siteIdDest`
(row 1) for the tour and cylinder folders below.

`siteId` is the **primary key**; the business keys are `SITE-CSPH-HQ`, `SITE-DEP-DLA-PRINCIPAL`,
`SITE-CLT-IND-RECEPTION` and friends (the `siteCode*` environment variables).

**organization-service on :8082**, with `X-User-PersonId` (required `@RequestHeader`).

`CreateSiteRequest` requires `code`, `siteId`, `name`, `organizationId` and `type`. Two unique constraints -
`Site.code` and `(organizationId, name)` - hence `{{uniq}}` in **both** `code` and `name`.

**organization-service on :8082**, no security headers, so `CLASS_VIEW` is bypassed.

Enveloped **array**. Read-only reference data - `ClassStructureController` declares a single `GET` and no write
method, so there is no create step for it in either collection.

item.description:
organization-service on **8082**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-organization-service` in-cluster.

Reads go out with **no security headers**, which is what makes `PermissionAspect` skip `ORG_VIEW` / `SITE_VIEW` /
`CLASS_VIEW`. Writes carry `X-User-PersonId` because those methods declare it as a required `@RequestHeader` - a
missing header there is a 400 from Spring MVC, never a 403.

**Response shapes:** `/organizations` and `/sites` are bare `PageResponse`s; `/organizations/{id}` and
`/classifications` are enveloped; `/organizations/{id}/children` is an enveloped array.

item.name: 03 - User  (direct -8083)

request.description:
**user-service on :8083**, no security headers, so `PERSON_VIEW` is bypassed.

**The trailing slash is required** - `PersonController` is `@GetMapping("/")`, and `/api/v1/persons` without it is a
404 even on the direct port.

**Bare `PageResponse`.** Resolves the logged-in user by business key and stores the **UUID** into `personIdNew`,
because every `/persons/{id}/...` path variable below wants the UUID while the `personId` variable holds a business
key (`superadmin.cspHq`).

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers. This method has no `@RequiresPermission` at all, so the header
question does not arise - it is open either way.

Business-key lookup (`/persons/by-person-id/{key}`) as opposed to the UUID lookup (`/persons/{id}`). The segment
order is the only thing that tells them apart, and it is the most common 404 in this API.

**user-service on :8083**, with **no security headers**.

`createPerson` declares `@RequestHeader(value = "X-User-PersonId", required = false)` - optional, unlike
organization-service''s writes. So the bypass applies cleanly here and the controller substitutes `"SYSTEM"` for the
audit field. That asymmetry between services is exactly what the direct-port collection makes visible.

`email` carries `{{uniq}}`; returns **200, not 201** (the handler returns `ApiResponse` directly).

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers - `PERSON_UPDATE` is bypassed.

`UpdatePersonRequest` has no `@NotBlank`, so an empty body is a legal request; the only hard requirement is the
person id in the path.

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers - `PERSON_UPDATE` is bypassed.

Same `{newStatus, reason}` contract as the organization call in folder `02`; the `UpdateStatusRequest` class name
recurs in both modules with a matching shape.

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers, so `ROLE_VIEW` is bypassed.

Queried by the person''s **business** `personId` internally, even though the path carries the UUID - the controller
resolves the person first. Empty for the person just created.

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers - `ROLE_UPDATE` is bypassed. The header is
`required = false` here, so the audit field falls back to `"SYSTEM"`.

`AssignRoleRequest` requires `personId` **and** `roleId` (`@NotBlank`). `personId` is the **business key** even
though the controller overwrites it - `@Valid` runs at binding time, before the body, so omitting it is a 400.

**Needs `{{roleId}}`.** Nothing in this collection creates a role, so seed it once from the gateway collection, or
send `GET :8083/api/v1/roles/` (below) and copy a `data[].id` into the environment variable. The test tolerates 400
for that reason rather than failing obscurely.

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers, so `PERMISSION_VIEW` is bypassed.

The **effective** permission set, flattened from every granted role by `PermissionService.resolvePermissions`. This
is the same computation `AuthService` runs at login to build the JWT `permissions` claim.

A `Set<String>` serialises as a JSON **array**, so the assertion expects an array rather than a `PageResponse`.

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers, so `ROLE_VIEW` is bypassed.

Enveloped **array**, not a `PageResponse` - despite `/persons/` two requests up being a bare page. Different
controller, different convention, same service.

Also the place to get a `roleId` if `{{roleId}}` is empty: copy any `data[].id` into the environment variable.

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers, so `ROLE_VIEW` is bypassed.

Only permissions whose grant row has `granted = true`; `RoleService.getPermissionsForRole` filters on that flag.
Enveloped **array**. Tolerates 404 for an unknown `roleId`.

**user-service on :8083**, no security headers, so `GROUP_VIEW` is bypassed.

Enveloped **array**, trailing slash required. Groups are permission bundles used for a bulk grant instead of
per-person role assignment; `memberCount` is maintained denormalised on the row.

item.description:
user-service on **8083**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-user-service` in-cluster.

No security headers anywhere in this folder - every method declares its `X-User-PersonId` with `required = false`, so
the audit field falls back to `"SYSTEM"` and the permission aspect is bypassed throughout. Contrast with folder `02`,
where organization-service''s writes make the header mandatory.

**Trailing slash required** on `/persons/` and `/roles/`. `/persons/` is a bare `PageResponse`; `/roles/` and
`/groups/` are enveloped arrays.

item.name: 04 - Tour  (direct -8086)

request.description:
**fleet-device-service on :8088**, called from the tour folder for one reason: `assign-vehicle` needs a `vehicleId`
and this collection does not create vehicles before the tour folder runs.

No security headers, so `fleet.vehicles.read` is bypassed. Enveloped `ApiResponse<PageResponse<VehicleResponse>>` -
note the **dotted lower-case** permission style this service uses, against UPPER_SNAKE elsewhere.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers, so `TOUR_VIEW` is bypassed. Enveloped `PageResponse`.

`TourResponseDto` nests its `checkpoints` inline, so one call can show the full itinerary shape.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers - `createTour` reads `X-User-Username` with `required = false`, so
`createdBy` ends up null. That is the honest difference from the gateway collection, where the JWT populates it.

`CreateTourDto` requires `tourCode`, `marketerOrganizationId`, `executionMode`, `type` and `requestedQuantity`
(`@NotNull @Positive`). `executionMode` is `INTERNAL` or `EXTERNAL`; `INTERNAL` adds a database constraint that a
transporter must be assigned, so `EXTERNAL` is used here.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers, so `TOUR_VIEW` is bypassed.

Compare `status` before and after the `start` request below - that pair shows the lifecycle actually moving without
a gateway anywhere in sight.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers - `TOUR_ASSIGN_VEHICLE` is bypassed.

**`vehicleId` is a REQUIRED query parameter** and this endpoint takes no body. Omitting it is a 400
`MissingServletRequestParameterException`, and the failure message says nothing about which parameter was expected -
so the assertion below logs the body when that happens.

`{{vehicleId}}` was seeded by the `GET :8088/api/v1/vehicles` request at the top of this folder.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers - `TOUR_START` is bypassed.

`DRAFT -> IN_PROGRESS`, with `startedAt` stamped server-side. No body, no parameters.

Starting a tour twice is a state-machine error, so the test tolerates 409/422 and reports the reason instead of
treating a legitimate refusal as a defect.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers - `TOUR_UPDATE` is bypassed.

Two database constraints shape the body:

* `chk_checkpoint_exclusive` - exactly one of `siteId` / `clientSiteId`, never both and never neither.
* `UNIQUE (tournee_id, sequence)` - one stop per position per tour. The tour is created fresh in this run, so
  `sequence: 1` is always free.

`sequence` is `@Min(1)`, and `tourId` is injected from the path - it must **not** appear in the body.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers - `CHECKPOINT_VALIDATE` is bypassed.

Marks the stop reached / delivered. **No body and no parameters** - this is exactly the route a driver''s PDA hits
on arrival, which is why it must stay parameterless.

Penalised by the reconciliation engine when the delivered quantity is short, which is what folder `07` measures.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers, so `PICKUP_VIEW` is bypassed. Enveloped `PageResponse`.

The demand side of a tour. Lifecycle: `DRAFT -> VALIDATED -> INPROGRESS -> COMPLETED` (or `CANCELLED`).

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers - `PICKUP_CREATE` reads `X-User-PersonId` with `required = false`, so
`createdBy` is null on a direct call.

`CreatePickupRequestDto` requires `marketerOrganizationId`, `sourceSiteId` and `destinationSiteId`; `requestedQuantity`
is `@Min(1)`. Site ids came from the folder `02` site list.

**tour-service on :8086**, no security headers - `PICKUP_APPROVE` is bypassed.

**`approvedQuantity` is a REQUIRED query parameter**, a primitive `double`: omitting it 400s, and so does sending
anything non-numeric.

11 against a requested 12 is deliberate - a CSPH agent routinely authorises less than a marketer asks for, and the
difference is the audit trail the subsidy workflow reconciles later.

item.description:
tour-service on **8086**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-tour-service` in-cluster.

No security headers anywhere in this folder - every tour-service method reads its identity header with
`required = false`, so the audit fields end up null on a direct call. That is a real, visible difference from the
gateway collection rather than a defect in either.

One cross-service request opens the folder: `GET :8088/api/v1/vehicles`, because `assign-vehicle` needs a
`vehicleId` and this collection does not create vehicles before this folder runs.

item.name: 05 - Cylinder  (direct -8087)

request.description:
**cylinder-service on :8087**, no security headers, so `CYLINDER_VIEW` is bypassed.

**Bare `PageResponse`** - no `success` envelope. Same shape through the gateway, which confirms the convention
belongs to the controller rather than to the route taken.

**cylinder-service on :8087**, no security headers - `createCylinder` reads `X-User-PersonId` with `required = false`.

`CreateCylinderRequest` requires only `serialNumber`; the ownership and location fields are what make the record
useful. `serialNumber` carries `{{uniq}}` because it is the bottle''s field identity.

**cylinder-service on :8087**, no security headers, so `CYLINDER_VIEW` is bypassed.

`CylinderResponse` is the join of the physical asset (serial, brand, capacity) and its administrative state (holder,
site, fill status) - "where is this bottle" and "is this bottle usable" are the same record.

**cylinder-service on :8087**, no security headers - `CYLINDER_TRANSFER` is bypassed.

**`targetSiteId` is a REQUIRED body field** (`@NotBlank`). Note the contrast with the tour service''s
`assign-vehicle` two folders up, which wanted its target in the *query string* - two conventions for "required
target" in the same codebase, and the body form is the more common one.

A transfer rewrites `currentHolderOrganizationId` and `currentSiteId` in one call: it is a custody change, not an
append to a movement log, and it should emit an audit event.

**cylinder-service on :8087**, no security headers, so `RFID_VIEW` is bypassed. **Bare `PageResponse`.**

`current_site_id` and `current_client_site_id` are mutually exclusive by check constraint - a tag is at an
operational site or a client site, never both. That is the same constraint the checkpoint body in folder `04`
enforces.

item.name: POST :8087/api/v1/rfid  (no headers needed; bottleSerial has a CHECK)

request.description:
**cylinder-service on :8087**, no security headers - `RFID_CREATE` reads `X-User-PersonId` with `required = false`.

`CreateRfidTagRequest` requires only `tagUid` - the EPC written into the tag''s memory.

**`bottleSerial` carries a database CHECK constraint: `^[A-Z0-9]{8,}$`** - uppercase alphanumeric only, at least 8
characters, no dashes. `BT` + a 15-character timestamp satisfies it; `BT-2026-01` would be rejected by Postgres rather
than by bean validation, which is a far worse error to debug. `tagUid` has no such constraint.

**cylinder-service on :8087**, no security headers, so `RFID_VIEW` is bypassed.

By **primary key**. The sibling route `/rfid/tag/{tagUid}` addresses the same resource by EPC - which is how a
handheld reader asks "what is this?", never "what is the id of the row whose id I already know".

**cylinder-service on :8087**, no security headers - `SCAN_CREATE` reads `X-User-PersonId` with `required = false`.

`CreateScanEventRequest` requires only `rfidTagId`; the rest is the evidence bundle that makes a scan admissible.
`scan_events.checkpoint_id` is `NOT NULL`, so **folder `04` must have run** - that is the one ordering dependency
this collection has.

`pdaSyncId` makes ingestion idempotent when a handheld reconnects after a blackspot and replays its buffer, which is
the normal case in the field rather than an edge case.

item.description:
cylinder-service on **8087**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-cylinder-service` in-cluster.

No security headers anywhere - every method here reads `X-User-PersonId` with `required = false`, so the audit field
falls back to null and `CYLINDER_*` / `RFID_*` / `SCAN_*` checks are bypassed.

**Both list routes are bare `PageResponse`s.** One ordering dependency: `POST /scans` needs a `checkpointId` from
folder `04`, because `scan_events.checkpoint_id` is `NOT NULL`.

item.name: 06 - Fleet  (direct -8088)

request.description:
**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers, so `fleet.vehicles.read` is bypassed.

Enveloped `ApiResponse<PageResponse<VehicleResponse>>` - note the **dotted lower-case** permission style this service
uses (`fleet.vehicles.read` / `.create` / `.write` / `.manage`) against UPPER_SNAKE in organization, user and tour
services. Both styles are live in the same `permissions` table.

Also the only list endpoint in the platform with a server-side sort contract (`sortBy` / `sortDir`).

**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers - `fleet.vehicles.create` is bypassed.

`CreateVehicleRequest` requires only `licensePlate`, and `vehicles.license_plate` is `VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE`. `DLT-` plus
the 15-character `{{uniq}}` is 18 characters - deliberately inside the limit, because an over-length plate is a 500
from the database rather than a 400 with a field name in it.

**201 Created** - `VehicleController.createVehicle` sets `HttpStatus.CREATED` explicitly, unlike most create endpoints
in the platform. The test asserts 201 exactly here.

**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers, so `fleet.vehicles.read` is bypassed.

`certificateExpiryAt` is the compliance field: an expired certificate is what a CSPH inspection actually checks, and
the platform surfaces it here rather than only in a report.

**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers, so `fleet.devices.read` is bypassed.

IoT devices: `GPS`, `PDA` or `RFIDREADER` (`DeviceType`), each optionally assigned to a person or a vehicle.
Enveloped `PageResponse`.

**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers - `fleet.devices.create` is bypassed.

`CreateDeviceRequest` requires `serialNumber` **and** `deviceType`; `devices.serial_number` is `VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE`.

The pairing of `batteryLevel` with the derived `batteryCritical` flag is how a low-battery handheld gets flagged
before it dies mid-tour. **201 Created**, like `/vehicles` and for the same reason.

**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers, so `fleet.devices.read` is bypassed.

`lastLatitude` / `lastLongitude` / `lastSync` are the cached position, deliberately separate from the telemetry
history: a device that stopped reporting looks identical to a stationary one unless you check `lastSync`.

**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers - `fleet.devices.write` is bypassed.

Assigns the device to a driver **and** a truck in one call, which is the real-world pairing: a handheld rides in a
specific truck with a specific person. `AssignDeviceRequest` has no `@NotBlank`, so assigning to nobody is legal
(if useless).

The counterpart `POST /devices/{id}/unassign` takes **no body at all** - the server nulls both columns itself, so
sending `{"assignedToPersonId": null}` is unnecessary and ignored.

**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers - `TELEMETRY_INGEST` is bypassed.

**The response is 201 with a completely EMPTY body** - `ResponseEntity.status(CREATED).build()` with no payload.
Calling `pm.response.json()` on it throws, so this request deliberately asserts on the status and the emptiness only.
This is the one place in either collection where a JSON assertion would be wrong.

**fleet-device-service on :8088**, no security headers, so `TELEMETRY_VIEW` is bypassed.

**The response is a BARE object, not an `ApiResponse` envelope** - `ResponseEntity<TelemetryResponse>` rather than
`ResponseEntity<ApiResponse<TelemetryResponse>>`. There is no `success` key and no `data` wrapper; the position
fields sit at the top level.

Three adjacent endpoints, three different response conventions. Worth knowing before writing a client against this
controller.

item.description:
fleet-device-service on **8088**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-fleet-device-service` in-cluster.

No security headers - this service uses the **dotted lower-case** permission style (`fleet.vehicles.read`,
`fleet.devices.write`, `TELEMETRY_VIEW`) and every one of those checks is bypassed here.

Three response conventions in three adjacent controllers: `/vehicles` and `/devices` are enveloped
`PageResponse`s, `POST /telemetry` answers 201 with an **empty body**, and `GET /telemetry/vehicles/{id}/latest`
answers a **bare object**.

item.name: 07 - Subsidy  (direct -8089)

request.description:
**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers, so the declaration read check is bypassed. Enveloped `PageResponse`.

Volume declarations: a marketer declares the volume it sold in a period. Lifecycle
`DRAFT -> SUBMITTED -> RECONCILED -> DISPUTED` (`DeclarationStatus`).

**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers. This service reads `X-User-Username` (not `X-User-PersonId`) with
`required = false`, so `createdBy` ends up null on a direct call.

`CreateDeclarationRequest` requires `periodStart` and `periodEnd` (`@NotNull`); `getEffectiveOrganizationId()` falls
back from `declaringOrganizationId` to `marketerOrganizationId`, so sending both is the explicit choice.

`declaredVolume` is what the marketer *claims* - the reconciliation below measures it against tracked volume.

**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers, so the declaration read check is bypassed.

The natural place to watch `status` and `statusDate` as the folder below walks the lifecycle.

**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers, so the submit check is bypassed.

`DRAFT -> SUBMITTED`. No body, no parameters.

Every later action (review, approve, reject) is only legal from `SUBMITTED`, so folder order is load-bearing here in a
way it is not for a plain CRUD resource.

**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers, so the review check is bypassed.

A CSPH agent reviews the declaration. Both query parameters are **optional** (`required = false`) - unlike
`assign-vehicle`, `skip` and `approvedQuantity` elsewhere - but a review with neither reviewer nor notes is useless,
so both are supplied.

This is the human checkpoint between the marketer''s claim and the regulator''s decision.

**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers, so the reconciliation read check is bypassed.

The regulator''s measured answer to the marketer''s claim. `reconciliations.declaration_id` is `UNIQUE`, so there is
at most one per declaration - which is why the by-declaration route can 404.

**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers. Only `declarationId` is required; every tracked figure is
optional.

The numbers are the whole point: 12.0 t declared against 12.0 t tracked here, but **one more bottle out than in** -
and `trackedBottlesOut - trackedBottlesIn` is the leak the redressement amount in the gateway collection is computed
from. `subsidyRate` is the per-tonne rate applied to the volume gap.

**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers, so the redressement read check is bypassed.

Redressements - the financial penalty owed when tracked volume falls short of declared volume. The last link in the
chain: declaration -> reconciliation -> redressement -> payment.

**subsidy-service on :8089**, no security headers. Requires `reconciliationId` (`@NotBlank`) and `dueDate`
(`@NotNull`); `amount` and `transactionRef` are optional.

625.0 is exactly one ton at the declared 625 per-tonne rate, which makes the figure checkable by hand - the property
that actually matters in a subsidy dispute.

`dueDate` comes from the collection pre-request (30 days out), so the penalty is never already overdue.

item.description:
subsidy-service on **8089**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-subsidy-service` in-cluster.

No security headers - this service reads `X-User-Username` with `required = false`, so `createdBy` is null on a
direct call.

**The chain is strictly ordered:** declaration -> reconciliation -> redressement, each link only accepting its own
predecessor''s identifier. Folder order is load-bearing, and the `submit` / `review` steps are only legal in that
sequence.

item.name: 08 - Audit  (direct -8084)

request.description:
**audit-service on :8084**, no security headers, so the audit read check is bypassed.

Field-level change history. Enveloped `ApiResponse<PageResponse<EntityModificationResponse>>`. Filters are bound
through an `AuditQueryParams` `@ModelAttribute`: `entityType`, `entityId`, `actorPersonId`, `action`, `module`,
`dateFrom`, `dateTo`, `page`, `size`.

A row is one entity modification whose nested `changes` list holds the individual before/after field pairs - the
granularity a GPL audit actually requires.

**audit-service on :8084**, no security headers, so the audit read check is bypassed.

The status-change journal: who moved which entity from which status to which, and when. Same
`AuditQueryParams` binding as `/modifications`, kept separate because status transitions are what regulators ask for
by name and are indexed differently.

**audit-service on :8084**, no security headers, so the audit read check is bypassed.

**Two path segments, and `entityType` is the entity''s type, not the API module.** Valid values are `ORGANIZATION`,
`SITE`, `PERSON`, `CYLINDER`, `RFID_TAG`, `TOUR`, `VEHICLE`, `DECLARATION` and so on. The module (`AUTH`, `TOUR`,
`FLEET`) is a different concept and a different field.

A wrong `entityType` 404s rather than returning an empty summary, so a typo here is loud rather than silent - which
is better than most of the platform.

**audit-service on :8084**, no security headers - the ingest endpoint declares no identity header at all.

**The body is a RAW `AuditEvent`, not wrapped in an `ApiResponse` envelope.** This is the one write endpoint in the
platform that takes a bare domain object; the response is enveloped as usual.

`AuditEvent` is what every microservice publishes on the broker after a write, and audit-service consumes it into
`EntityModification` + `FieldChange` rows. This endpoint is the synchronous equivalent - useful for replaying events
and for testing ingestion without a broker.

The field is `actionDescription`; note that `AuthService` sends `description` instead, and both exist on the DTO -
another small inconsistency in the same audit surface. Both are sent here so the event is complete either way.

body.raw:
{
  "entityType": "ORGANIZATION",
  "entityId": "{{orgId}}",
  "entityName": "Postman Direct Org {{uniq}}",
  "action": "UPDATE",
  "actionDescription": "Direct-port ingest probe",
  "description": "Emitted by csph-services-direct on :8084",
  "module": "ORGANIZATION",
  "changeby": "{{personId}}",
  "changedate": "{{nowIso}}",
  "changes": [
    { "fieldName": "status", "fieldLabel": "Statut", "oldValue": "INACTIVE", "newValue": "ACTIVE", "valueType": "STRING" }
  ],
  "deviceInfo": "Postman-direct",
  "ipAddress": "127.0.0.1"
}

item.description:
audit-service on **8084**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-audit-service` in-cluster.

No security headers - the audit read checks are bypassed and `POST /ingest` declares no identity header at all.

All three reads are **enveloped** `PageResponse`s, so this folder is internally consistent even though the platform
is not. The write takes a **raw** `AuditEvent` rather than an enveloped body.

item.name: 09 - Notification  (direct -8085)

request.description:
**notification-service on :8085**, no security headers. This controller declares no identity header at all.

`CreateTemplateRequest` marks **every** field `@NotBlank` - code, name, subject, bodyTemplate, module, channel,
language. That is the strictest create DTO in the platform, and the 400 message names the offending field.

`code` is the business key used by `/notifications/send`, so it carries `{{uniq}}`.

`bodyTemplate` uses `{{placeholder}}` syntax (double braces) resolved at send time against the request''s
`variables`. An unresolved placeholder is left in the body **verbatim with no error** - which is worth remembering
the next time a notification arrives containing a literal `{{reference}}`.

**The body sends `\{\{recipientName\}\}` with escaped braces, and that matters.** Postman substitutes `{{...}}` in
request bodies before sending, so an unescaped placeholder would become an empty string and the stored template
would silently lose its slots. `\{\{` is how you send a literal `{{`.

body.raw:
{
  "code": "DIR-TPL-{{uniq}}",
  "name": "Postman Direct Template {{uniq}}",
  "subject": "Notification directe {{uniq}}",
  "bodyTemplate": "Bonjour \{\{recipientName\}\}, votre demande \{\{reference\}\} est \{\{status\}\}. - Postman direct probe",
  "module": "TOUR",
  "channel": "EMAIL",
  "language": "FR"
}

request.description:
**notification-service on :8085**, no security headers.

The whole template catalogue. Enveloped **array** - never paged, because the catalogue is small and static.

`language` is part of the template, so a French and an English variant are two distinct rows with two distinct
codes. This list is the place to check whether a translation actually exists before chasing a "wrong language
notification" report.

**notification-service on :8085**, no security headers.

Addressed by **business `code`** - there is no `/{id}` route in this controller, so a UUID here is a guaranteed 404.
`{{templateCode}}` is captured by the create request above and is empty on a cold run, which the test tolerates.

**notification-service on :8085**, no security headers.

**`recipientEmail` is deliberately NOT sent.** It is optional, and when absent `NotificationService` logs
`Channel EMAIL not supported or missing email for ...`, skips the SMTP call, and the endpoint still answers
**200**. That keeps this request working with a local MailHog - or with no SMTP server at all - which is the point of
a repeatable suite.

If you do add `recipientEmail`, the send attempts real SMTP against `spring.mail.host` (`MAIL_HOST`, default
`smtp.gmail.com:587`). Any failure is caught and recorded as `status: FAILED` on the log row, and the endpoint still
answers 200 - so check `j.data.status`, not the HTTP code, to know what happened. Captured mail shows up at
`{{mailhogWeb}}` (MailHog UI, default :8026).

The `variables` map is what fills the `{{placeholder}}` slots in the template body.

item.description:
notification-service on **8085**, i.e. `http://csph/gpl-notification-service` in-cluster.

No security headers - this controller declares no identity header on any method, so there is nothing for the
permission aspect to bypass.

Templates are addressed by **business `code`**, never by UUID. `POST /notifications/send` omits `recipientEmail` on
purpose so no SMTP connection is attempted and the endpoint answers a clean 200.

item.name: 10 - Permission AOP contrast

request.description:
## The demonstration, step 1 of 3

Same endpoint, same `@RequiresPermission("ORG_VIEW")`, **no security headers at all**.

`PermissionAspect.checkPermission` starts with:

```java
if (!GplSecurityContext.isAuthenticated()) {
    return joinPoint.proceed();   // "internal call, pass-through"
}
```

`GplSecurityContextFilter` only calls `GplSecurityContext.set(...)` when `X-User-PersonId` is present and non-empty,
so with no header there is no context, `isAuthenticated()` is false, and the aspect proceeds. **200.**

This is exactly what an in-cluster `http://csph/gpl-organization-service/...` call does, and it is the reason this
collection exists.

## The demonstration, step 2 of 3

**Identical request to A, plus one header: `X-User-PersonId`.**

Now `GplSecurityContextFilter` builds a context, `isAuthenticated()` is true, and the aspect evaluates
`hasPermission("ORG_VIEW")` against the (empty) permission set - so it throws `AccessDeniedException` and
`GlobalExceptionHandler` maps it to **403**.

One header, and a `200` becomes a `403`. That is the whole mechanism in a single diff, and it is why the direct-port
collection omits the header on reads: sending it accidentally turns an exploration call into a permission test.

403 bodies **are** enveloped JSON, unlike the gateway's plain-text 401s.

## The demonstration, step 3 of 3

Identical to B, plus **`X-User-Permissions: ORG_VIEW`**. The aspect now finds the permission in the context set and
grants access: **200**.

And this is the security consequence worth stating plainly: **on a direct port, a caller can assert any permission
it likes by setting the header.** The headers are trusted because in production only the gateway sets them - the
gateway validates the JWT, then injects `X-User-PersonId` / `X-User-Roles` / `X-User-Permissions` itself, replacing
anything a client sent.

That is also why the service containers must **not** be exposed outside the cluster. This request is safe here
because it only ever runs against `localhost` in development; the same request against a pod IP reachable from
outside would be a privilege-escalation path.

The three requests together are the whole security model in nine lines of Postman.

item.description:
Three requests against **one** endpoint, differing only in their security headers. Together they are the whole
permission model:

| | `X-User-PersonId` | `X-User-Permissions` | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | absent | absent | **200** - `PermissionAspect` finds no context and passes through |
| **B** | present | absent | **403** - context exists, permission missing |
| **C** | present | `ORG_VIEW` | **200** - permission found |

The corollary, stated in request C''s description and worth repeating: the headers are **trusted**, so the service
ports must never be reachable from outside the cluster. A caller who can reach :8082 directly can simply assert
whatever permission it wants.
